data.title: Income Investors Should Know That Johnson & Johnson (NYSE:JNJ) Goes Ex-Dividend Soon
data.description:
Regular readers will know that we love our dividends at Simply Wall St, which is why it's exciting to see Johnson & Johnson (NYSE:JNJ) is about to trade ex-dividend in the next 4 days. The ex-dividend date is one business day before a company's record date, which is the date on which the company determines which shareholders are entitled to receive a dividend. The ex-dividend date is important as the process of settlement involves a full business day. So if you miss that date, you would not show up on the company's books on the record date. In other words, investors can purchase Johnson & Johnson's shares before the 24th of November in order to be eligible for the dividend, which will be paid on the 8th of December.

The company's next dividend payment will be US$1.34 per share, and in the last 12 months, the company paid a total of US$5.36 per share. Last year's total dividend payments show that Johnson & Johnson has a trailing yield of 2.0% on the current share price of US$272.70. If you buy this business for its dividend, you should have an idea of whether Johnson & Johnson's dividend is reliable and sustainable. As a result, readers should always check whether Johnson & Johnson has been able to grow its dividends, or if the dividend might be cut.

AI is about to change healthcare. These 20 stocks are working on everything from early diagnostics to drug discovery. The best part - they are all under $10bn in marketcap - there is still time to get in early.

Dividends are typically paid from company earnings. If a company pays more in dividends than it earned in profit, then the dividend could be unsustainable. Its dividend payout ratio is 79% of profit, which means the company is paying out a majority of its earnings. The relatively limited profit reinvestment could slow the rate of future earnings growth. We'd be concerned if earnings began to decline. That said, even highly profitable companies sometimes might not generate enough cash to pay the dividend, which is why we should always check if the dividend is covered by cash flow. Dividends consumed 63% of the company's free cash flow last year, which is within a normal range for most dividend-paying organisations.

It's positive to see that Johnson & Johnson's dividend is covered by both profits and cash flow, since this is generally a sign that the dividend is sustainable, and a lower payout ratio usually suggests a greater margin of safety before the dividend gets cut.

Check out our latest analysis for Johnson & Johnson

Click here to see the company's payout ratio, plus analyst estimates of its future dividends.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?

Businesses with strong growth prospects usually make the best dividend payers, because it's easier to grow dividends when earnings per share are improving. If earnings decline and the company is forced to cut its dividend, investors could watch the value of their investment go up in smoke. With that in mind, we're encouraged by the steady growth at Johnson & Johnson, with earnings per share up 3.6% on average over the last five years. A high payout ratio of 79% generally happens when a company can't find better uses for the cash. Combined with slim earnings growth in the past few years, Johnson & Johnson could be signalling that its future growth prospects are thin.

Many investors will assess a company's dividend performance by evaluating how much the dividend payments have changed over time. Johnson & Johnson has delivered an average of 6.0% per year annual increase in its dividend, based on the past 10 years of dividend payments. We're glad to see dividends rising alongside earnings over a number of years, which may be a sign the company intends to share the growth with shareholders.

To Sum It Up

Is Johnson & Johnson an attractive dividend stock, or better left on the shelf? Earnings per share growth has been unremarkable, and while the company is paying out a majority of its earnings and cash flow in the form of dividends, the dividend payments don't appear excessive. In summary, while it has some positive characteristics, we're not inclined to race out and buy Johnson & Johnson today.

However if you're still interested in Johnson & Johnson as a potential investment, you should definitely consider some of the risks involved with Johnson & Johnson. Our analysis shows 2 warning signs for Johnson & Johnson and you should be aware of these before buying any shares.

Generally, we wouldn't recommend just buying the first dividend stock you see. Here's a curated list of interesting stocks that are strong dividend payers.

data.title: Why Owning AbbVie Through ETFs Could Change The Risks You Carry
data.description:
Anyone buying AbbVie stock directly takes on its company-specific risks alone. Simply Wall St notes that AbbVie carries a high level of debt and that its dividend of 2.55% is not well covered by earnings. Owning AbbVie through a fund that also holds other healthcare businesses spreads out how much those issues can influence your overall portfolio, and also limits how much AbbVie’s individual performance can drive your results.

A recent development is news on 19 November 2026 that AbbVie is teaming up with DISCO Pharmaceuticals to work on new bispecific drugs for solid tumors. The deal brings an upfront payment to DISCO and gives AbbVie another path to cancer treatments, which could be relevant for its long-term oncology mix. Investors who want AbbVie within a broader basket can consider funds such as XLV, VHT and HDV as ways to gain that exposure.

Rather choose individual stocks than a fund? Explore 35 high quality undervalued stocks.

State Street Health Care Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLV)

XLV is built around large health stocks, with pharmaceuticals at 37.2% and biotechnology at 19.9% of the portfolio. Health care equipment, tools and services, managed care and distributors make up most of the rest. AbbVie is the third largest position at 7.64%, so about US$76 of every US$1,000 you put into XLV goes into AbbVie. The two bigger holdings are Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson, which together account for about 26.8% of the fund and have a significant influence on overall results.

AbbVie’s high level of debt is specific to its own balance sheet. XLV partly softens that single company risk because other holdings such as Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson rely on their own capital structures, product ranges and cash flows, not AbbVie’s. Sector concentration is the main drawback, because you still depend on how large health care stocks as a group respond to regulation, pricing pressure and sentiment toward the industry.

Not every stock inside XLV is priced the same way. Find out how many of XLV's holdings look undervalued.

Vanguard Health Care ETF (VHT)

Life sciences tools and services play a bigger role in VHT than in XLV, with meaningful exposure to equipment makers and research providers alongside large drugmakers. The ETF still closely resembles XLV overall, since about 87% of its holdings overlap, and Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson together make up just over one fifth of the fund. AbbVie is the third largest position at 6.73%, so roughly US$67 of every US$1,000 invested in VHT is tied to AbbVie rather than its peers.

Negative shareholders equity at AbbVie would be a company-level balance sheet issue. VHT can limit how much that single risk affects an investor’s money because it spreads the rest of the capital across hundreds of other health businesses, including firms focused on equipment, tools and managed care that respond more to procedure volumes and insurance trends than AbbVie’s own finances.

Uncover whether VHT has kept pace with the market over the past week, year and five years

iShares Core High Dividend ETF (HDV)

HDV gives AbbVie real weight without letting it dominate your money. AbbVie is about 6.91% of the portfolio, so each US$1,000 puts roughly US$69 into the stock, and the rest into other high dividend companies. ExxonMobil Holdings is the largest position, and together with AbbVie makes up 15.8% of the fund. Beyond those two, the ETF leans on Integrated Oil and Gas, Tobacco, Soft Drinks and Non-alcoholic Beverages, Electric Utilities and other sectors. This creates exposure that stretches well beyond health care.

AbbVie’s dividend of 2.55% is not well covered by earnings, which leaves income investors exposed if the payout ever has to be reset. HDV partly cushions that specific weakness by owning other cash generating sectors such as Integrated Oil and Gas and Household Products that rely on their own demand and pricing. Future dividend policies across the portfolio still depend on how each underlying business performs and what its board decides.

See what you'd actually own if you bought HDV, from its 80 positions to how much sits in the top 10.

Choosing how you want AbbVie exposure

You are really picking what you want around AbbVie, not between tiny or massive stakes. XLV and HDV each put just under US$80 of every US$1,000 into AbbVie, with VHT closer to US$70, and all three charge about US$8 to US$9 a year on a US$10,000 holding. XLV and VHT cluster around large health businesses, and VHT spreads your money across far more holdings than XLV. HDV mixes AbbVie with energy, consumer and telecom stocks, so your risk is less tied to health care regulation. Recent cancer drug work with DISCO sits inside all of that. The real question is simple: do you want AbbVie mainly alongside health stocks, or as part of a wider income portfolio?

Eli Lilly is the largest holding in both XLV and VHT, so you'd own it either way. Check whether Eli Lilly trades above or below its fair value.

data.title: What Xiaomi Bears Saw Before The Fall
data.description:
If you had looked at Xiaomi on 1 January 2026 and decided to sit it out, the move might feel easier to justify now. For Xiaomi shareholders, the loss from the start of the year was 29.2%, including dividends. That decline came alongside rising memory costs, heavier EV losses, and softer smartphone demand reported later in the period. The real question is which early assumptions about margins, capital intensity, or market maturity were already on record before any of that news arrived.

Narratives are how investors here put a case on the record, with explicit assumptions about revenue, margins and the multiple. Those assumptions imply an estimated Fair Value.

Xiaomi is not the only name tied to this theme. Zero in on 33 elite gold producer stocks and compare how each one is priced.

The Two Xiaomi Stories Investors Had To Weigh

The shares cost HK$39.3 at the start of the period, and anyone considering Xiaomi then had to choose between two sharply different expectations for where the business might be headed.

The bullish narrative saw a Fair Value of HK$66.01, or 68% above the start price. It leaned on Xiaomi pushing deeper into premium smartphones, appliances, and EVs, with analysts assuming 21.3% revenue growth and a 9.1% profit margin over a 3 year horizon.

The bearish case put Fair Value at HK$35.12, or 11% below the start price. That view focused on smartphone saturation and heavier research spending, with analysts in that camp assuming 16.5% revenue growth and a profit margin drifting to 7.6% over roughly the same period.

What The Results Changed For The Xiaomi Thesis

Xiaomi’s later report showed Q2 2026 revenue at C¥108,921.609m and net income at C¥9,462.405m, both below Q2 2025, with net margin sliding from 10.3% to 8.7%. That outcome leaned toward the cautious case on profitability. News of rising memory costs, EV losses and a profit slump reinforced that pressure, so the period cut both ways for the original narratives.

The lesson is simple. When a story leans on margin expansion, track the reported net margin and segment level cost lines rather than only top line growth or product launches.

What Xiaomi's Drop Leaves You Paying For Today

Xiaomi now trades at HK$28.52, with this Narrative's Fair Value sitting above that level. The analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St frames that gap around Xiaomi's ability to use its Mobile × AIoT ecosystem and premium hardware to reshape its mix.

A buyer today would be assuming heavy AI, EV and R&D spending ultimately turns into durable monetisation across devices, software and higher margin internet services rather than staying mostly a cost line.

"The main thing that has to go right is that heavy long term spending on AI, embodied intelligence and smart EVs, including the planned R&D ramp, converts into sustained monetisation across devices, services and autos rather than remaining a cost drag."

Another Way Into Xiaomi's Theme

Xiaomi keeps pulling you toward devices, ecosystems and how people upgrade. One step away, a different business leans on a similar consumer habit.

Your phone and watch are becoming a personal hub for media, payments and health tracking. That shift depends on buyers accepting premium hardware to access richer subscription services.

One large consumer tech group is pushing that model hard. It uses custom chips, higher end devices and bundled apps to steer users deeper into paid services.

If more spending tilts from hardware to subscriptions over time, that pattern could matter. Especially for any company already sitting inside your pocket and on your wrist.

data.title: We're Keeping An Eye On NorthWest Copper's (CVE:NWST) Cash Burn Rate
data.description:
We can readily understand why investors are attracted to unprofitable companies. For example, although software-as-a-service business Salesforce.com lost money for years while it grew recurring revenue, if you held shares since 2005, you'd have done very well indeed. Nonetheless, only a fool would ignore the risk that a loss making company burns through its cash too quickly.

So, the natural question for NorthWest Copper (CVE:NWST) shareholders is whether they should be concerned by its rate of cash burn. A company's cash runway is the amount of time it would take to burn through its cash reserves at its current cash burn rate. In June 2026, NorthWest Copper had CA$10m in cash, and was debt-free. Looking at the last year, the company burnt through CA$7.8m. So it had a cash runway of approximately 16 months from June 2026. That's not too bad, but it's fair to say the end of the cash runway is in sight, unless cash burn reduces drastically. You can see how its cash balance has changed over time in the image below.

How Is NorthWest Copper's Cash Burn Changing Over Time?

NorthWest Copper didn't record any revenue over the last year, indicating that it's an early stage company still developing its business. So while we can't look to sales to understand growth, we can look at how the cash burn is changing to understand how expenditure is trending over time. Remarkably, it actually increased its cash burn by 220% in the last year. With that kind of spending growth its cash runway will shorten quickly, as it simultaneously uses its cash while increasing the burn rate. Admittedly, we're a bit cautious of NorthWest Copper due to its lack of significant operating revenues. We prefer most of the stocks on this list of stocks that analysts expect to grow.

How Easily Can NorthWest Copper Raise Cash?

Given its cash burn trajectory, NorthWest Copper shareholders may wish to consider how easily it could raise more cash, despite its solid cash runway. Issuing new shares, or taking on debt, are the most common ways for a listed company to raise more money for its business. Many companies end up issuing new shares to fund future growth. By looking at a company's cash burn relative to its market capitalisation, we gain insight on how much shareholders would be diluted if the company needed to raise enough cash to cover another year's cash burn.

Since it has a market capitalisation of CA$62m, NorthWest Copper's CA$7.8m in cash burn equates to about 13% of its market value. As a result, we'd venture that the company could raise more cash for growth without much trouble, albeit at the cost of some dilution.

Is NorthWest Copper's Cash Burn A Worry?

data.title: Sanford Limited Just Beat EPS By 14%: Here's What Analysts Think Will Happen Next

Sanford Limited (NZSE:SAN) just released its annual report and things are looking bullish. It was overall a positive result, with revenues beating expectations by 6.6% to hit NZ$599m. Sanford reported statutory earnings per share (EPS) NZ$0.80, which was a notable 14% above what the analysts had forecast. The analysts typically update their forecasts at each earnings report, and we can judge from their estimates whether their view of the company has changed or if there are any new concerns to be aware of. So we collected the latest post-earnings statutory consensus estimates to see what could be in store for next year.

Following last week's earnings report, Sanford's two analysts are forecasting 2027 revenues to be NZ$606.2m, approximately in line with the last 12 months. Statutory earnings per share are expected to sink 17% to NZ$0.66 in the same period. In the lead-up to this report, the analysts had been modelling revenues of NZ$584.1m and earnings per share (EPS) of NZ$0.68 in 2027. Overall it looks as though the analysts were a bit mixed on the latest results. Although there was a to revenue, the consensus also made a small dip in its earnings per share forecasts.

Check out our latest analysis for Sanford

The consensus price target was unchanged at NZ$7.95, suggesting the business is performing roughly in line with expectations, despite some adjustments to profit and revenue forecasts.

Another way we can view these estimates is in the context of the bigger picture, such as how the forecasts stack up against past performance, and whether forecasts are more or less bullish relative to other companies in the industry. It's pretty clear that there is an expectation that Sanford's revenue growth will slow down substantially, with revenues to the end of 2027 expected to display 1.3% growth on an annualised basis. This is compared to a historical growth rate of 3.2% over the past five years. By way of comparison, the other companies in this industry with analyst coverage are forecast to grow their revenue at 6.5% per year. Factoring in the forecast slowdown in growth, it seems obvious that Sanford is also expected to grow slower than other industry participants.

The Bottom Line

The biggest concern is that the analysts reduced their earnings per share estimates, suggesting business headwinds could lay ahead for Sanford. They also upgraded their revenue estimates for next year, even though it is expected to grow slower than the wider industry. The consensus price target held steady at NZ$7.95, with the latest estimates not enough to have an impact on their price targets.
